title: What are ligaments?
intro: Ligaments are strong bands of fibrous tissue that connect bones to other bones and stabilise joints. They guide movement and prevent joints from moving too far. Injuries to ligaments, called sprains, are common, particularly in the ankle, knee and wrist.

sections.heading: Structure and function
paragraphs: Ligaments are made mainly of collagen fibres, arranged in parallel bundles that give strength while allowing a little elasticity. They hold bones together at joints, limit abnormal movement, and contain nerve endings that help the brain sense joint position, which contributes to balance. They are different from tendons, which connect muscle to bone.

sections.heading: Important ligaments
paragraphs: In the knee, the cruciate ligaments inside the joint control forward and backward movement and rotation, and the collateral ligaments on the sides stabilise it from side to side. In the ankle, ligaments on the outer side are those most often sprained. Other examples include ligaments of the wrist, shoulder and spine.

sections.heading: Sprains and tears
paragraphs: A sprain is a stretch or tear of a ligament. Grade one is a mild stretch, grade two a partial tear and grade three a complete rupture. Symptoms include pain, swelling, bruising, tenderness and instability. Many sprains heal with rest, protection, early gentle movement and physiotherapy, while complete tears of some ligaments may need surgery.

sections.heading: Healing and care
paragraphs: Ligaments have a limited blood supply, so they heal slowly, over weeks to months, and may not return to full strength. Rehabilitation to restore movement, strength and balance reduces re-injury. Some people have loose ligaments, called hypermobility, which can cause joint pain or instability. Strengthening muscles around the joint offers extra support.

sections.heading: Preventing injury
paragraphs: Warm up before exercise, build strength and balance, use proper technique and footwear, and increase training gradually. Braces or tape can be used for a time after injury or in high-risk sports. See a doctor for severe pain, inability to bear weight, marked swelling or a joint that gives way.

examples.title: Recovering from a sprain
examples.text: Imagine you sprained your ankle. You could rest and protect it for the first days, start gentle movement as pain allows and practise balance exercises.

examples.title: Preventing recurrence
examples.text: Suppose you often twist your ankle. You might ask a physiotherapist for a balance programme and advice on supportive shoes.
